hook.text: A boring meeting drags for hours. An exciting game ends in minutes. Same time, different perception.

buildup.text: The brain has no single clock organ. It constructs time from neural oscillations, attention, and memory.

discovery.text: More events processed per interval makes time feel longer. A novel experience fills more memory, stretching perceived duration.

twist.text: In a car accident, time seems to slow—but experiments show your clock doesn't speed up. Memory just records more detail.

climax.text: Dopamine modulates time perception. Stimulants make time feel faster; depressants make it crawl.

quiz.question: Why does time seem to slow during emergencies?

details.summary: Time perception is constructed by the brain and is surprisingly flexible. Time seems to slow during danger, speed up when you are engaged, and compress in memory for routine periods. There is no single brain clock; multiple systems estimate duration depending on the timescale involved.
details.whyItMatters: Time is not experienced objectively. Understanding time perception explains why some experiences feel long while they happen but short in memory, and vice versa.
takeaways: Time perception is constructed, not passively recorded
Different brain systems handle different timescales
Emotional arousal and attention strongly distort time perception

faq.question: Why does time seem to slow down during scary events?
faq.answer: Recent research suggests time does not actually slow in the moment. Instead, the brain encodes more details during high-arousal events, and richer memories are later interpreted as having lasted longer. In real-time tests, people do not gain improved temporal resolution during fear.

faq.question: Why do years seem shorter as you get older?
faq.answer: Novel experiences create detailed memories. Childhood is full of first experiences. As an adult, routine life creates fewer distinct memories. When you look back, fewer memories make the period feel shorter. Vacations to new places feel long in retrospect because they are rich in novel memories.
